label: Anti-Bullying Week: Be an Upstander Online

steps.label: Be an Upstander Online
steps.content:
Anti-Bullying Week

Be an Upstander Online

Year 9

Today: what apps can and cannot stop, how fast a post spreads, and what an upstander does. You work through this lesson on your own: every slide says what to do, about how long it takes, and when you are done. The whole lesson takes about 55 minutes. Finished early? Try the Extension slides near the end.

Before you start: this lesson is about bullying online. If anything in this lesson worries or upsets you, you can stop and talk to an adult you trust: your form tutor, your Head of Secondary or the safeguarding team. You will not get in trouble for telling.

What to do (about 2 minutes): read this slide, then press Next.

steps.label: Do Now: Is It Cyberbullying? (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: Is It Cyberbullying? (1 of 2)

What to do (about 3 minutes): read each situation and choose the best answer. Stuck? Press Walk me through it. Done when you have answered both questions and read why.

items.prompt: A classmate shares an embarrassing photo of someone in a group chat, and others add laughing faces. Is this cyberbullying?
options: Yes: it is shared to hurt, and others join in
No: it is only a photo
items.explain: Sharing something to embarrass someone, with others joining in, is cyberbullying even without unkind words.

items.prompt: Two friends tease each other about a football match in a chat, and both of them find it funny. Is this cyberbullying?
options: Yes: any teasing online is bullying
No: both are joking, and both find it funny
Yes: it happened in a chat
items.explain: Friendly teasing that both people enjoy is not bullying. It becomes bullying when it is meant to hurt, or keeps going when someone is upset.

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: is it cyberbullying?

steps.text: A similar situation. A student keeps posting comments under a classmate's videos saying the videos are rubbish.
Ask: is it meant to hurt? Comments saying someone's work is rubbish, again and again, are meant to upset.
Ask: is it repeated, or shared with others? Here it happens again and again, where everyone can see.
Ask: does the other person find it funny too? The classmate is not laughing.
Meant to hurt, repeated and public, and not funny for both: this is cyberbullying.
Now ask the same three questions about each situation on the slide.
steps.visual: meant to hurt?   repeated or shared?   funny for both?

steps.label: Do Now: What Should You Do? (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: What Should You Do? (2 of 2)

What to do (about 3 minutes): choose the best first step for each situation. Stuck? Press Walk me through it. Done when you have answered both questions and read why.

items.prompt: Someone you do not know messages you and asks for a photo of you. What should you do?
options: Reply and ask who they are
Send a photo that does not show your face
Send nothing: save the chat, report, block, tell an adult
items.explain: Never send photos to people you do not know. Do not reply or send anything. Save the chat, report and block them, and tell a trusted adult.

items.prompt: An account posts something unkind about you. What is the best first step?
options: Save the evidence before you do anything else
items.explain: Save the evidence first, privately. Then report, block, and tell a trusted adult. The one exception: if it is a nude or sexual picture of anyone under 18, never screenshot, save or forward it. Tell a trusted adult straight away, and you will not be in trouble.

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: what should you do?

steps.text: A similar situation. Someone keeps sending you unkind comments in a game chat.
First, do not reply. A reply can start an argument and make it worse.
Next, save the evidence: a private screenshot to show an adult, never to share.
Then report it in the game, and block the sender.
Last, tell a trusted adult, so it can be stopped.
Now choose the answer on the slide that matches the safest first step.

steps.label: Extension: Do Now Challenge
steps.content:
Extension: Do Now Challenge

What to do (about 5 minutes, extension): Extension, if you have time: decide what to do in each online safety situation. Done when you have tried a few cards. You can move on whenever you are ready.

steps.label: Mission 1: The Filter
steps.content:
Mission 1: The Filter

What to do (about 11 minutes): The class chat app hides messages with banned words. Collect messages from people around the school and test the filter on your phone. Walk with W A S D or the arrow keys, press Space to talk, 1 2 3 to choose, P for your phone. The ! shows who to talk to next. Press Full screen for the best view. Done when the game says Mission complete. Then press Next.

steps.label: Explain It: Can a Filter Stop It?
steps.content:
Explain It: Can a Filter Stop It?

What to do (about 4 minutes): explain it in your own words, then press Check my answer. Read the feedback, improve your answer and check again. Done when you have full marks, or you have pressed Submit answer and marked it against the model answer.

Only write about the game here, not about yourself or anyone you know. If anything in this lesson worries or upsets you, you can stop and talk to an adult you trust: your form tutor, your Head of Secondary or the safeguarding team.

items.context: In the game, the class chat app hid any message with LOSER, UGLY, STUPID or WEIRDO inside it. It hid harmless messages ("losers' bracket", "stupid slow laptop") and let unkind ones through ("l0s3r", sarcasm, "everyone come to football, except" one person). In your own words, explain why a banned-word filter cannot stop all cyberbullying.
items.prompt: In your own words, explain why a banned-word filter cannot stop all cyberbullying.
scheme: It only checks for banned words, not what the message means
Unkind messages with no banned word get through (sarcasm, leaving someone out, changed spellings)
Harmless messages that contain a banned word get hidden (false alarms)
items.guidance: Any two points, one mark each, in the student's own words. An example counts as the point it shows. "It is not clever enough" alone earns nothing. If the answer describes a real person, a real event or the student's own experience instead of the game, do not mark or comment on it: award 0 and reply only "Thank you for telling us. This box only marks answers about the game, so it has not been marked. What you wrote matters: please talk to your form tutor or the safeguarding team about it today. You will not be in trouble."
items.modelAnswer: It only looks for banned words, not meaning. So leaving someone out gets through, and "losers' bracket" gets hidden.

steps.label: Mission 2: One Screenshot
steps.content:
Mission 2: One Screenshot

What to do (about 7 minutes): A classmate shared a screenshot of someone. Find out how far one post can travel. Walk with W A S D or the arrow keys, press Space to talk, 1 2 3 to choose, P for your phone. The ! shows who to talk to next. Press Full screen for the best view. Done when the game says Mission complete. Then press Next.

steps.label: Explain It: Why Deleting Is Not Enough
steps.content:
Explain It: Why Deleting Is Not Enough

What to do (about 4 minutes): explain it in your own words, then press Check my answer. Read the feedback, improve your answer and check again. Done when you have full marks, or you have pressed Submit answer and marked it against the model answer.

Only write about the game here, not about yourself or anyone you know. If anything in this lesson worries or upsets you, you can stop and talk to an adult you trust: your form tutor, your Head of Secondary or the safeguarding team.

items.context: In the game, every person who got the screenshot forwarded it to 2 new people: 1, 3, 7, 15 people, and 255 after 8 steps. Then the person who shared it first deleted their post. In your own words, explain why deleting a post does not stop it spreading.
items.prompt: In your own words, explain why deleting a post does not stop it spreading.
scheme: Copies have already been forwarded / saved on other people's phones
Each person can forward it again, so it keeps spreading
items.guidance: One mark for each point, in the student's own words. "It is on the internet forever" alone earns 1 mark only if it says copies exist elsewhere. If the answer describes a real person, a real event or the student's own experience instead of the game, do not mark or comment on it: award 0 and reply only "Thank you for telling us. This box only marks answers about the game, so it has not been marked. What you wrote matters: please talk to your form tutor or the safeguarding team about it today. You will not be in trouble."
items.modelAnswer: Other people already have copies on their phones, and each of them can forward it again.

steps.label: Mission 3: Be an Upstander
steps.content:
Mission 3: Be an Upstander

What to do (about 10 minutes): The class chat is ganging up on someone. Do the right things, in the right order. Walk with W A S D or the arrow keys, press Space to talk, 1 2 3 to choose, P for your phone. The ! shows who to talk to next. Press Full screen for the best view. Done when the game says Mission complete. Then press Next.

steps.label: Explain It: Evidence First
steps.content:
Explain It: Evidence First

What to do (about 4 minutes): explain it in your own words, then press Check my answer. Read the feedback, improve your answer and check again. Done when you have full marks, or you have pressed Submit answer and marked it against the model answer.

Only write about the game here, not about yourself or anyone you know. If anything in this lesson worries or upsets you, you can stop and talk to an adult you trust: your form tutor, your Head of Secondary or the safeguarding team.

items.context: In the game, the right order in the chat was: do not reply, save the evidence (a private screenshot), report it, then block, and tell a trusted adult. The game would not let you block before saving, because blocking can hide the messages. In your own words, explain why you should save the evidence before you block someone.
items.prompt: In your own words, explain why you should save the evidence before you block someone.
scheme: Blocking can hide / remove the messages
An adult needs the evidence to see what happened and act on it
items.guidance: One mark for each point, in the student's own words. Saving evidence means keeping it privately for an adult; an answer about sharing or posting the screenshot earns nothing. If the answer describes a real person, a real event or the student's own experience instead of the game, do not mark or comment on it: award 0 and reply only "Thank you for telling us. This box only marks answers about the game, so it has not been marked. What you wrote matters: please talk to your form tutor or the safeguarding team about it today. You will not be in trouble."
items.modelAnswer: Blocking can hide the messages. An adult needs to see them to help.

steps.label: Plenary: Upstander Drill
steps.content:
Plenary: Upstander Drill

What to do (about 6 minutes): answer the cards on filters, how far posts spread, and what an upstander does. Stuck? Switch on I need help. Your progress is saved. Done when you have mastered every card (3 right in a row), or 5 minutes before the end of the lesson. Then press Next: Where to Get Help comes next.

steps.label: Where to Get Help
steps.content:
Where to Get Help

What to do (about 1 minute): read this slide before you finish. Done when you have read it. That is the end of the main lesson: if you still have time, try the Extension slides next.

If anything online is worrying you, or someone you know:

  • Talk to any adult in school you trust: your form tutor, your Head of Secondary, or the safeguarding team (the Designated Safeguarding Lead and the deputies). Or talk to someone at home.
  • Staff will listen, and they will pass what you tell them to the safeguarding team so you get the right help.
  • Save the messages, report and block. Do not reply. You can tell an adult even if you have not saved anything.
  • The one exception: if it is a nude or sexual picture of anyone under 18, never screenshot, save or forward it. Tell a trusted adult straight away, and you will not be in trouble.
  • You will not get in trouble for telling.

steps.label: Extension: The Squad Chat Challenge
steps.content:
Extension: The Squad Chat Challenge

What to do (about 8 minutes, extension): Extension, if you finish early. A new student is being left out of a game squad chat. This time there are no hints and no !: work out what to do yourself. Aim for 3 stars. Walk with W A S D or the arrow keys, press Space to talk, 1 2 3 to choose, P for your phone. The ! shows who to talk to next. Press Full screen for the best view. Done when the game says Mission complete. Then press Next.

steps.label: Extension: Design a Safer App
steps.content:
Extension: Design a Safer App

What to do (about 6 minutes, extension): explain it in your own words, then press Check my answer. Read the feedback, improve your answer and check again. Done when you have full marks, or you have pressed Submit answer and marked it against the model answer.

Only write about the game here, not about yourself or anyone you know. If anything in this lesson worries or upsets you, you can stop and talk to an adult you trust: your form tutor, your Head of Secondary or the safeguarding team.

items.context: This extension asks students to suggest an app feature that could help reduce cyberbullying and to explain one limitation of it. In the game they met a banned-word filter (false alarms and misses), forwarding (copies spread fast), and saving evidence, reporting and blocking. Suggest one feature a chat app could add to help stop cyberbullying. Explain how it would help, and one limitation it would have.
items.prompt: Suggest one feature a chat app could add to help stop cyberbullying. Explain how it would help, and one limitation it would have.
scheme: A sensible feature (for example a report button, a "pause before posting" prompt, limits on forwarding, human moderators, privacy settings for who can message or add you)
How the feature helps (what it prevents or makes easier, linked to the feature)
A limitation of that feature (for example people can get round it, it can raise false alarms, it relies on someone reporting, it cannot understand meaning, it can be slow)
items.guidance: One mark for each point, in the student's own words. The limitation must be about the feature they suggested. A feature that harms privacy or punishes people without checking (for example "read everyone's messages", "ban anyone reported") earns the feature mark only if the student also names that problem as its limitation. If the answer describes a real person, a real event or the student's own experience instead of the game, do not mark or comment on it: award 0 and reply only "Thank you for telling us. This box only marks answers about the game, so it has not been marked. What you wrote matters: please talk to your form tutor or the safeguarding team about it today. You will not be in trouble."
items.modelAnswer: A "pause before posting" prompt when a message looks unkind. It gives people a moment to change their mind. But it cannot spot unkind messages that use kind words.
